subject: Culture
title: Digital Afterlives
description: A micro-lesson that makes Digital Afterlives usable.

hook.text: Facebook has over 30 million profiles of dead people. By 2070, dead users may outnumber living ones.

buildup.text: Digital estates include email, social media, crypto wallets, and cloud storage. Death creates an inheritance problem.

discovery.text: AI chatbots trained on a dead person's texts can mimic conversation. Families talk to synthetic copies of the deceased.

twist.text: South Korea created a VR experience where a mother 'met' her deceased daughter in a virtual garden. She cried on camera.

climax.text: We're building digital ghosts without cultural frameworks to manage them. Technology outpaced the rituals we need.

punchline.text: The dead now live longer online than they did in the ground.

quiz.question: How many dead people have Facebook profiles?

details.summary: Technology is creating new kinds of afterlife — social media profiles of the dead persist indefinitely, AI chatbots mimic deceased loved ones, and digital memorial services maintain online shrines. The dead now have digital presence that previous generations could never have imagined.
details.whyItMatters: Digital afterlives raise unprecedented ethical questions about consent, grief, and memory. When AI can simulate a dead person's voice and personality, the boundary between honoring and exploiting the dead blurs.
takeaways: Facebook hosts over 30 million profiles of deceased users
AI companies now offer chatbots trained on deceased people's data
Digital estates and online legacy planning are growing legal fields

faq.question: What happens to social media accounts after death?
faq.answer: Facebook allows memorialization (adding 'Remembering' before the name) or deletion. Google has an Inactive Account Manager that can share or delete data. Many platforms lack clear death policies. Without planning, accounts may persist indefinitely or become inaccessible to family.

faq.question: Can AI bring back the dead?
faq.answer: Companies like HereAfter AI and StoryFile create interactive AI chatbots from recordings of living people for use after death. Others use text messages and social media posts to simulate the deceased's personality.
